title: Coral and the Bell
premise: Ada Hartwell, a pest controller with a habit of counting doors and keeping lights burning, is hired to deal with something in the drowned village of Marrow Fen that leaves fingerprints in frost, flour, and blood. Beneath the fen, an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, and the thing behind it begins borrowing the shapes and memories of the living, growing stronger with each recollection it steals. Ada discovers her own family took something from the fen in 1974—a bell, and with it a name—and that the entity's hunger is an inheritance she can no longer refuse. To survive the frost's final pattern, Ada must descend past the sealed door and return the bell, accepting that the price is her own memory of everyone she loves.
about_author: V. M. Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the property records of flooded English villages. Their fiction has appeared in several small-press horror anthologies, though they insist the best material never made it out of the reading room.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Frost
chapters.summary: Ada Hartwell arrives at Marrow Fen's last occupied farmhouse to investigate a 'pest problem' and finds handprints pressed into frost on the inside of sealed windows—prints too large for any resident. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional routine; her door-counting habit hints at an old, private fear.

chapters.title: The Village That Isn't
chapters.summary: Ada surveys the drowned village, learning Marrow Fen was deliberately flooded in 1974 and its church never demolished. The farmer's daughter, Nell, admits the prints started the day the excavation crew arrived. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: creeping dread as the professional job curdles into something personal.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Ada's first night in the farmhouse: she keeps every light burning and counts doors at intervals, a ritual she's never explained even to herself. At 3 a.m. the count comes up one door too many. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: intimate terror; her coping mechanism becomes evidence against her sanity.

chapters.title: The Excavation Crew
chapters.summary: Ada meets the crew draining a section of fen for a road bypass: brash foreman Dekker, nervous surveyor Idris, and site archaeologist Ruth, who shows her sonar readings of a structure beneath the water. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: ambition tinged with guilt—Ruth knows they shouldn't be digging here.

chapters.title: Something with Teeth in the Silt
chapters.summary: The dredger brings up livestock bones arranged in a spiral, and Idris finds a 1974 parish ledger listing a 'removal'—an object taken from the church, name redacted. That night the crew's generator dies and frost blooms inside their cabins. POV: Idris. Emotional beat: the crew's confidence fractures; denial begins to cost.

chapters.title: The Door, Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: The crew exposes an oak door standing upright in the drained fenbed, its hinges fused, its planks scarred by clawing from within. Ada recognizes the grain—it matches the extra door in her farmhouse. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: vertigo; the impossible has been waiting for her specifically.

chapters.title: What Nell Remembers
chapters.summary: Elderly Nell recalls the night in 1974 when her father and Ada's grandfather rowed something heavy out to the church before the floodwaters came. She remembers a bell that rang underwater for three days. POV: Nell. Emotional beat: grief and complicity; the older generation's silence exposed as survival.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Shape
chapters.summary: Dekker's missing crewmate returns—but he remembers nothing before last Tuesday and hums a hymn no one taught him. Ada notices the frost prints now match her own hands. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: violation; the entity is learning to wear the living.

chapters.title: Parish Records and Redactions
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Ada and Ruth find the 1974 file: the church bell was removed to stop the ringing, and the removal required 'a keeper of the count'—a role her grandfather held. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: inheritance as curse; her rituals were never hers alone.

chapters.title: The Bell in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's trail, Ada finds the bell crated in a derelict boathouse, its bronze skin crawling with frost ferns. When she touches it, she hears her own voice counting doors. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: dread of recognition—the bell knows her.

chapters.title: Idris Goes Under
chapters.summary: Idris, obsessed with the sonar shapes, wades into the fen at night. Ruth finds his clothes folded neatly on the bank and, beneath the ice, his face looking up—smiling, from below. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: guilt made flesh; the crew's excavation has opened a debt.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes
chapters.summary: Frost patterns now spell names across every surface in the farmhouse—first the dead, then the crew, then Ada's own name, half-finished. Nell warns: when the pattern completes, the door opens from both sides. POV: Nell. Emotional beat: countdown pressure; the supernatural acquires a deadline.

chapters.title: Dekker's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dekker tries to dynamite the door and the boathouse both. The explosion opens a crater but the door stands untouched in the smoke, and the entity speaks through Dekker's radio in Ada's grandfather's voice, offering to 'let the count end' if she abandons the bell. POV: Dekker. Emotional beat: power's corruption—the entity recruits through fear and flattery.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Count
chapters.summary: Ada finds her grandfather's journal: keepers of the count maintained the bell's exile by remembering the drowned village daily, feeding the entity memory to keep it asleep. He stopped in 1974 and passed the duty down unexplained. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: bitter inheritance; her whole life was a ritual she didn't know she was performing.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth admits she pushed the excavation through despite the parish warnings, seduced by the career-making find. She offers to help Ada return the bell, but Ada catches frost prints matching Ruth's boots leading toward the door. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: shame and suspicion—has Ruth already been borrowed?

chapters.title: The Long Cold Night
chapters.summary: The entity stops borrowing and begins erasing: Nell forgets her daughter's name, Ada loses the memory of her mother's face, and every clock in Marrow Fen stops at 3:04 a.m.—the hour of the 1974 flood. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: grief in advance; memory itself becomes the battlefield.

chapters.title: Across the Frozen Fen
chapters.summary: Ada and Ruth haul the bell by sledge across the ice toward the standing door as frost closes in like a written sentence completing itself. Dekker follows, half-borrowed, pleading and threatening by turns. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: grim resolve; a funeral march across the ice.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Both Ways
chapters.summary: At the door, the entity wears Ada's grandfather's shape and offers a trade: the bell for her memories of everyone she loves. Ruth steps forward to take the bargain instead—and Ada realizes the Ruth beside her was borrowed miles back. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: betrayal and clarity; she must grieve the living.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Ada rings the bell against the door. The true Ruth surfaces from the fen, gasping, and together they swing the bell until the bronze cracks and the door swings inward on darkness that remembers everything. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: climax; sacrifice through sound, giving the entity back its own name.

chapters.title: The Name in the Bronze
chapters.summary: Inside the threshold, Ada sees the entity as it was: the village's drowned bell-ringer, sealed in by his own neighbors in 1974, kept nameless so he could not rest. She speaks his name—taken from the bell's inscription—and the frost pattern stops mid-letter. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: terrible compassion; the monster was made by the village's own corruption of power.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: The fen refills overnight, door and all. Dekker is found alive but remembering nothing; Ruth's report lists the site as archaeologically insignificant. Ada wakes with the bell's crack scarred into her palm—and no memory of her mother's face, the price already paid. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: hollow victory; the record is sanitized, the cost invisible.

chapters.title: The Count Begins Again
chapters.summary: Months later, Ada takes a routine call in another fen-edge village and finds frost prints on the inside of a window. She keeps the lights on and counts the doors—twice—and writes her grandfather's journal anew, adding her own entry: keeper of the count, third of her line. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: quiet dread and acceptance; inheritance continues, and she chooses to carry it knowingly.
